title: CN-lab-01: Network Namespace Inspecting
markdown:
# CN-lab-01: Network Namespace Inspecting

Every container runtime you will ever touch — Docker, containerd, Kubernetes' CRI — relies on one Linux kernel primitive to give each container its own private network stack: the **network namespace**. Before connecting namespaces to anything, you need to actually see one from the inside: what exists in it the moment it's created, what's missing, and how running a command "inside" a namespace is fundamentally different from running it on the host.

This lab is pure observation. You will create a namespace, inspect it, and delete it — no connectivity yet. That comes in the next lab (CN-lab-02).

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Create and delete network namespaces with `ip netns add` / `ip netns delete`
- List existing namespaces with `ip netns list`
- Run commands inside a namespace with `ip netns exec`
- Explain what a freshly created namespace contains (and doesn't)
- Contrast a namespace's interface list with the host's

## What Is a Network Namespace, Really?

A network namespace is a Linux kernel feature that gives a process group its own, completely isolated copy of the networking stack: its own interfaces, its own routing table, its own ARP cache, its own firewall rules. By default, every process on a Linux machine lives in the single "root" (or "default") namespace — the one your SSH session is in right now. `ip netns add` creates a *new*, empty one, sitting alongside the root namespace, sharing nothing network-related with it until you explicitly connect the two.

This is precisely the mechanism `docker run` uses under the hood: every container gets its own network namespace, which is why `eth0` can exist independently inside a dozen different containers on the same host without conflicting — each `eth0` lives in its own namespace.

## Part 1: Creating and Listing a Namespace

### Step 1: Create a Namespace

```bash
sudo ip netns add inspect-ns
```

This creates the namespace and, behind the scenes, a bind-mounted file under `/var/run/netns/inspect-ns` that represents it — that file is what lets `ip netns exec` find it later.

### Step 2: List Namespaces

```bash
ip netns list
```

`inspect-ns` should appear. If you try to create a namespace with a name that already exists, `ip netns add` fails with `File exists` — namespace names must be unique, just like filenames in a directory.

## Part 2: Looking Inside

### Step 1: Inspect the Namespace's Interfaces

Every command you want to run *inside* a namespace — rather than on the host — gets prefixed with `ip netns exec <name>`. This is the standard, modern replacement for the older `nsenter` tool: both ultimately attach the following command to the namespace's network stack, but `ip netns exec` is built into `iproute2` and is what you'll see in almost every up-to-date runbook.

```bash
sudo ip netns exec inspect-ns ip link show
```

You will see exactly **one** interface: `lo`, the loopback — and it will be in `DOWN` state. That's it. No `eth0`, no veth, nothing. A freshly created namespace is about as empty as a Linux network stack can be: no routes, no ARP entries, no firewall rules, and even its own loopback isn't active yet.

Compare that against the host:

```bash
ip link show
```

The host shows every real and virtual interface that exists outside the namespace — `lo`, `eth0`, and whatever else the machine has. Nothing you see here exists inside `inspect-ns`, and nothing inside `inspect-ns` is visible from here. That's the isolation guarantee a namespace gives you: two processes, one on each side, cannot even see each other's interfaces, let alone talk to each other, until you deliberately build a bridge between them (literally, in CN-lab-06).

### Step 2: Bring the Namespace's Loopback Up

Even `lo` — normally always-on, taken for granted on the host — starts `DOWN` inside a new namespace and has to be brought up explicitly, just like any other interface:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec inspect-ns ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec inspect-ns ip link show lo
```

You'll now see `lo` reporting `LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP`. This matters more than it looks: plenty of software inside a container (or namespace) assumes `127.0.0.1` works — and it silently doesn't, until `lo` is brought up. This is one of the first things container runtimes do when setting up a new network namespace for you, invisibly.

**Why it matters**: when a container's local health check or an internal `localhost:PORT` connection mysteriously fails on a minimal/from-scratch container runtime, a down loopback inside its namespace is a real, if rare, culprit — and now you know exactly what command fixes it.

## Part 3: Cleaning Up

```bash
sudo ip netns delete inspect-ns
ip netns list
```

Deleting a namespace removes it and everything inside it — any interfaces still living there (there are none yet in this lab) would simply cease to exist. `ip netns list` should no longer show `inspect-ns`.

## Conclusion

A network namespace starts as close to nothing as the kernel allows: one loopback interface, down, with no routes and no rules. Everything else — real interfaces, addresses, routing, connectivity to the outside world — has to be built deliberately, piece by piece. That's exactly what the rest of this module does: CN-lab-02 connects a namespace to the host with a veth pair, CN-lab-05 connects two namespaces directly to each other, and CN-lab-06 connects several namespaces through a shared bridge. Understanding that a namespace is *isolated by default, connected by choice* is the one idea every other lab in this module builds on.
